claim: Salinamide A (SalA) and salinamide B (SalB) are structurally related bicyclic depsipeptide antibiotics, each consisting of seven amino acids and two non-amino-acid residues.
source: Salinamide A (Sal; SalA) and salinamide B (SalB) are structurally related bicyclic depsipeptide antibiotics, each consisting of seven amino acids and two non-amino-acid residues (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore et al., 1999; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore et al., 1999) and reference to Figure 1A showing structures.

claim: SalA and SalB are produced by Streptomyces sp. CNB-091, a marine bacterium isolated from the surface of the jellyfish Cassiopeia xamachana.
source: SalA and SalB are produced by Streptomyces sp. CNB-091, a marine bacterium isolated from the surface of the jellyfish Cassiopeia xamachana (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore and Seng, 1998; Moore et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore and Seng, 1998; Moore et al., 1999).

claim: SalA is also produced by Streptomyces sp. NRRL 21611, a soil bacterium.
source: SalA also is produced by Streptomyces sp. NRRL 21611, a soil bacterium (Miao et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Miao et al., 1997).

claim: SalA and SalB exhibit antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial pathogens, particularly Enterobacter cloacae and Haemophilus influenzae.
source: SalA and SalB exhibit antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial pathogens, particularly Enterobacter cloacae and Haemophilus influenzae, but do not exhibit cytotoxicity against mammalian cells (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore et al., 1999; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore et al., 1999) and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SalA and SalB do not exhibit cytotoxicity against mammalian cells.
source: SalA and SalB exhibit antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial pathogens, particularly Enterobacter cloacae and Haemophilus influenzae, but do not exhibit cytotoxicity against mammalian cells (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore et al., 1999; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Trischman et al., 1994; Moore et al., 1999) and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SalA and SalB inhibit both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) in vitro.
source: SalA and SalB inhibit both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) in vitro, but do not inhibit human RNAP I, II, or III in vitro (Miao et al., 1997; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Miao et al., 1997) and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SalA and SalB do not inhibit human RNAP I, II, or III in vitro.
source: SalA and SalB inhibit both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial RNA polymerase (RNAP) in vitro, but do not inhibit human RNAP I, II, or III in vitro (Miao et al., 1997; Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Miao et al., 1997) and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A total synthesis of SalA has been reported.
source: A total synthesis of SalA has been reported (Tan and Ma, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Tan and Ma, 2008).

claim: Addition of Sal to bacterial cultures inhibits RNA synthesis at the first time point following addition.
source: The results in Figure 2A shows that addition of Sal to cultures inhibits RNA synthesis at the first time point following addition and inhibits protein synthesis at later time points.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Addition of Sal to bacterial cultures inhibits protein synthesis at later time points.
source: The results in Figure 2A shows that addition of Sal to cultures inhibits RNA synthesis at the first time point following addition and inhibits protein synthesis at later time points.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Addition of Sal has no effect on DNA synthesis in bacterial cultures.
source: Addition of Sal has no effect on DNA synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The pattern of macromolecular synthesis inhibition observed for Sal matches the pattern observed for the reference RNAP inhibitor rifampin.
source: The pattern observed for Sal matches the pattern observed for the reference RNAP inhibitor rifampin (Rif; compare red lines and blue lines in Figure 2A; Lancini and Sartori, 1968; Lancini et al., 1969)
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 2A and citations to prior work on rifampin (Lancini and Sartori, 1968; Lancini et al., 1969).

claim: Sal inhibits RNA synthesis in bacterial cells in culture.
source: We conclude that Sal inhibits RNA synthesis in bacterial cells in culture, and we infer that Sal inhibits RNAP in bacterial cells in culture.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Sal inhibits RNAP in bacterial cells in culture.
source: We conclude that Sal inhibits RNA synthesis in bacterial cells in culture, and we infer that Sal inhibits RNAP in bacterial cells in culture.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing RNA synthesis inhibition.

claim: Spontaneous Sal-resistant mutants were isolated with a frequency of approximately 1 × 10−9.
source: Spontaneous Sal-resistant mutants were isolated with a frequency of ∼1 × 10−9 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 100% (47/47) of the analyzed Sal-resistant mutants were found to contain mutations in genes for RNAP subunits.
source: Strikingly, 100% (47/47) of the analyzed Sal-resistant mutants were found to contain mutations in genes for RNAP subunits: 36 were found to contain mutations in rpoC and 11 were found to contain mutations in rpoB (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sequencing of Sal-resistant mutants shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 36 Sal-resistant mutants were found to contain mutations in rpoC.
source: Strikingly, 100% (47/47) of the analyzed Sal-resistant mutants were found to contain mutations in genes for RNAP subunits: 36 were found to contain mutations in rpoC and 11 were found to contain mutations in rpoB (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sequencing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 11 Sal-resistant mutants were found to contain mutations in rpoB.
source: Strikingly, 100% (47/47) of the analyzed Sal-resistant mutants were found to contain mutations in genes for RNAP subunits: 36 were found to contain mutations in rpoC and 11 were found to contain mutations in rpoB (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sequencing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A total of 21 different substitutions conferring Sal-resistance were identified.
source: A total of 21 different substitutions conferring Sal-resistance were identified (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Substitutions conferring Sal-resistance were obtained at 11 sites in RNAP β′ subunit (residues 690, 697, 738, 748, 758, 763, 775, 779, 780, 782, and 783).
source: Substitutions were obtained at 11 sites in RNAP β′ subunit (residues 690, 697, 738, 748, 758, 763, 775, 779, 780, 782, and 783) and three sites in RNAP β subunit (residues 569, 675, and 677) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Substitutions conferring Sal-resistance were obtained at three sites in RNAP β subunit (residues 569, 675, and 677).
source: Substitutions were obtained at 11 sites in RNAP β′ subunit (residues 690, 697, 738, 748, 758, 763, 775, 779, 780, 782, and 783) and three sites in RNAP β subunit (residues 569, 675, and 677) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All Sal-resistant mutants exhibited at least moderate-level (≥16-fold) resistance to SalA and SalB.
source: Quantitation of resistance levels indicated that all mutants exhibited at least moderate-level (≥16-fold) resistance to SalA and SalB, and that nine mutants exhibited high-level (≥128-fold) resistance to SalA (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Nine Sal-resistant mutants exhibited high-level (≥128-fold) resistance to SalA.
source: Quantitation of resistance levels indicated that all mutants exhibited at least moderate-level (≥16-fold) resistance to SalA and SalB, and that nine mutants exhibited high-level (≥128-fold) resistance to SalA (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Transfer of plasmids carrying plasmid-borne, induced Sal-resistant mutants was found to transfer the Sal-resistant phenotype.
source: Transfer of plasmids carrying plasmid-borne, induced Sal-resistant mutants was found to transfer the Sal-resistant phenotype, indicating that no mutation outside of rpoC or rpoB is required for Sal-resistance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from plasmid transfer experiments.

claim: No mutation outside of rpoC or rpoB is required for Sal-resistance.
source: Transfer of plasmids carrying plasmid-borne, induced Sal-resistant mutants was found to transfer the Sal-resistant phenotype, indicating that no mutation outside of rpoC or rpoB is required for Sal-resistance.
evidence: Inference based on plasmid transfer experiments showing that plasmid-borne mutations alone confer resistance.

claim: A single substitution in an RNAP subunit gene, either rpoC or rpoB, is sufficient to confer Sal-resistance.
source: From the analysis of spontaneous and induced Sal-resistant mutants, we conclude that a single substitution in an RNAP subunit gene, either rpoC or rpoB, is sufficient to confer Sal-resistance, and we infer that RNAP is the functional cellular target for Sal.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analysis of spontaneous and induced mutants.

claim: RNAP is the functional cellular target for Sal.
source: From the analysis of spontaneous and induced Sal-resistant mutants, we conclude that a single substitution in an RNAP subunit gene, either rpoC or rpoB, is sufficient to confer Sal-resistance, and we infer that RNAP is the functional cellular target for Sal.
evidence: Inference based on genetic data showing that mutations in RNAP genes confer resistance.

claim: The sites of substitutions conferring Sal-resistance form a tight cluster in the three-dimensional structure of RNAP.
source: In the three-dimensional structure of RNAP, the sites of substitutions conferring Sal-resistance form a tight cluster ('the Sal target'; green surface in Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The dimensions of the Sal target are approximately 35 Å × 18 Å × 12 Å.
source: The dimensions of the Sal target are ∼35 Å × ∼18 Å × ∼12 Å.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis of the Sal target.

claim: The Sal target is sufficiently large to be able to encompass Sal (approximately 16 Å × 12 Å × 10 Å).
source: The Sal target is sufficiently large to be able to encompass Sal (∼16 Å × ∼12 Å × ∼10 Å).
evidence: Inference based on comparison of dimensions of Sal target and Sal molecule.

claim: The Sal target is the binding site for Sal on RNAP.
source: Based on the observation that substitutions of the Sal target result in Sal-resistance (Figure 3A), we infer that the Sal target is the binding site for Sal on RNAP.
evidence: Inference based on genetic and structural data.

claim: The Sal target is located adjacent to, and partly overlaps, the RNAP active-center region.
source: The Sal target is located adjacent to, and partly overlaps, the RNAP active-center region (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sal likely inhibits RNAP by inhibiting RNAP active-center function.
source: We infer that Sal likely inhibits RNAP by inhibiting RNAP active-center function.
evidence: Inference based on the location of the Sal target adjacent to the active center.

claim: The Sal target does not overlap the RNAP active-center catalytic Mg2+ ion.
source: Mapping of substitutions conferring Sal-resistance onto the three-dimensional structure of a transcription elongation complex comprising RNAP, DNA, RNA, and an NTP (Vassylyev et al., 2007b) indicates that the Sal target does not overlap the RNAP active-center catalytic Mg2+ ion and does not overlap the RNAP residues that interact with the DNA template, the RNA product, and the NTP substrate.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis using the structure from Vassylyev et al., 2007b.

claim: The Sal target does not overlap the RNAP residues that interact with the DNA template, the RNA product, and the NTP substrate.
source: Mapping of substitutions conferring Sal-resistance onto the three-dimensional structure of a transcription elongation complex comprising RNAP, DNA, RNA, and an NTP (Vassylyev et al., 2007b) indicates that the Sal target does not overlap the RNAP active-center catalytic Mg2+ ion and does not overlap the RNAP residues that interact with the DNA template, the RNA product, and the NTP substrate.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis using the structure from Vassylyev et al., 2007b.

claim: Sal likely inhibits RNAP active-center function allosterically, through effects on RNAP conformation.
source: We infer that Sal likely inhibits RNAP active-center function allosterically, through effects on RNAP conformation, and not through direct, steric interactions with the RNAP residues that mediate bond formation, template binding, product binding, or substrate binding.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis showing Sal target does not overlap catalytic residues.

claim: The Sal target overlaps an RNAP active-center module referred to as the 'bridge-helix cap'.
source: The Sal target overlaps an RNAP active-center module referred to as the 'bridge-helix cap', which, in turn, comprises three active-center subregions: the 'bridge-helix N-terminal hinge' (BH-HN), the 'F-loop', and the 'link region' (Figure 3B; active-center subregion nomenclature as in Weinzierl 2010 and Hein and Landick 2010).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3B and nomenclature from Weinzierl 2010 and Hein and Landick 2010.

claim: 18 of the 21 identified substitutions conferring Sal-resistance map to the bridge-helix N-terminal hinge, F-loop, and link region.
source: 18 of the 21 identified substitutions conferring Sal-resistance, and all substitutions conferring high-level Sal-resistance, map to these RNAP active-center subregions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All substitutions conferring high-level Sal-resistance map to the bridge-helix N-terminal hinge, F-loop, and link region.
source: 18 of the 21 identified substitutions conferring Sal-resistance, and all substitutions conferring high-level Sal-resistance, map to these RNAP active-center subregions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The BH-HN undergoes conformational changes coupled to, and essential for, the nucleotide-addition cycle in transcription initiation and elongation.
source: It recently has been proposed that the BH-HN undergoes conformational changes coupled to, and essential for, the nucleotide-addition cycle in transcription initiation and transcription elongation, and that the F-loop, and possibly the link region, control these conformational changes (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).

claim: The F-loop, and possibly the link region, control conformational changes of the BH-HN.
source: It recently has been proposed that the BH-HN undergoes conformational changes coupled to, and essential for, the nucleotide-addition cycle in transcription initiation and transcription elongation, and that the F-loop, and possibly the link region, control these conformational changes (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).

claim: The BH-HN segment comprising β′ residues 779–783 undergoes a hinge-opening/hinge-closing conformational cycle coupled to the nucleotide-addition cycle.
source: Specifically, it has been proposed that the BH-HN segment comprising β′ residues 779–783—a segment that includes the sites of 6 of the 21 identified substitutions conferring Sal-resistance, and 4 of the 9 substitutions conferring high-level Sal-resistance—undergoes a hinge-opening/hinge-closing conformational cycle coupled to the nucleotide-addition cycle (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).

claim: Sal inhibits RNAP active-center function by inhibiting the proposed BH-HN hinge-opening and/or hinge-closing.
source: Based on the strong, nearly one-for-one, correspondence between the Sal target and the active-center subregions proposed to mediate and control the BH-HN hinge-opening/hinge-closing conformational cycle, we suggest that Sal inhibits RNAP active-center function by inhibiting the proposed BH-HN hinge-opening and/or hinge-closing.
evidence: Inference based on the correspondence between Sal target and BH-HN functional regions.

claim: The Sal target does not overlap the targets of the previously characterized RNAP inhibitors rifampin, streptolydigin, CBR703, myxopyronin, and lipiarmycin.
source: The Sal target does not overlap the targets of the previously characterized RNAP inhibitors Rif (Ovchinnikov et al., 1981, 1983; Lisitsyn et al., 1984; Jin and Gross, 1988; Severinov et al., 1993, 1994; Campbell et al., 2001; Garibyan et al., 2003), streptolydigin (Stl; Lisitsyn et al., 1985; Heisler et al., 1993; Severinov et al., 1993, 1995; Tuske et al., 2005; Temiakov et al., 2005), CBR703 (Artsimovitch et al., 2003; X Wang and RHE, unpublished), myxopyronin (Myx; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Srivastava et al., 2011), and lipiarmycin (Lpm; Ebright, 2005; Tupin et al., 2010; Srivastava et al., 2011) (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4A and citations to prior work on other RNAP inhibitors.

claim: The Sal target is located adjacent to, but does not overlap, the Rif, Stl, and CBR703 targets.
source: The Sal target is located adjacent to, but does not overlap, the Rif, Stl, and CBR703 targets.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Sal target is distant from the Myx and Lpm targets.
source: The Sal target is distant from the Myx and Lpm targets.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sal-resistant mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with Rif, Stl, CBR703, Myx, and Lpm.
source: Consistent with the absence of overlap between the Sal target and the Rif, Stl, CBR703, Myx, and Lpm targets, Sal-resistant mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with Rif, Stl, CBR703, Myx, and Lpm (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rif-resistant, Stl-resistant, CBR703-resistant, Myx-resistant, and Lpm-resistant mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with Sal.
source: Conversely, Rif-resistant, Stl-resistant, CBR703-resistant, Myx-resistant, and Lpm-resistant mutants do not exhibit cross-resistance with Sal (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For approximately one-quarter to one-half of Sal-resistant substitutions, there is significant (≥ fourfold) hyper-susceptibility to Stl and CBR703.
source: For approximately one-quarter to one-half of Sal-resistant substitutions, not only is there no cross-resistance to Stl and CBR703, but also there is significant (≥ fourfold) hyper-susceptibility to Stl and CBR703 (data in blue in Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Sal may inhibit a different RNAP reaction step than Stl and CBR703.
source: We infer that Sal may inhibit a different RNAP reaction step than Stl and CBR703 and/or may bind to and stabilize a different RNAP conformational state than Stl and CBR703.
evidence: Inference based on the observation of hyper-susceptibility to Stl and CBR703 in Sal-resistant mutants.

claim: Sal may bind to and stabilize a different RNAP conformational state than Stl and CBR703.
source: We infer that Sal may inhibit a different RNAP reaction step than Stl and CBR703 and/or may bind to and stabilize a different RNAP conformational state than Stl and CBR703.
evidence: Inference based on the observation of hyper-susceptibility to Stl and CBR703 in Sal-resistant mutants.

claim: Co-administration of Sal (resistance rate = 2 × 10−9 per generation) and Rif (resistance rate = 1 × 10−9 per generation) results in a resistance rate below the limit of detection (<2 × 10−12 per generation).
source: Thus, co-administration of Sal (resistance rate = 2 × 10−9 per generation) and Rif (resistance rate = 1 × 10−9 per generation) results in a resistance rate below the limit of detection (<2 × 10−12 per generation).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Co-administration of Sal (resistance rate 2 × 10−9 per generation) and Myx (resistance rate 3 × 10−10 per generation) results in a resistance rate below the limit of detection (<2 × 10−12 per generation).
source: In the same manner, co-administration of Sal (resistance rate 2 × 10−9 per generation) and Myx (resistance rate 3 × 10−10 per generation) results in a resistance rate below the limit of detection (<2 × 10−12 per generation).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Sal does not inhibit formation of a heparin-resistant RNAP-promoter open complex.
source: The results in Figure 5A show that Sal does not inhibit formation of a heparin-resistant RNAP-promoter open complex.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanisms of transcription inhibition by Myx and Lpm.
source: The results indicate that the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanisms of transcription inhibition by Myx and Lpm, both of which inhibit the formation of the RNAP-promoter open complex (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Tupin et al., 2010; Srivastava et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing Sal does not inhibit open complex formation, combined with citations showing Myx and Lpm do inhibit this step.

claim: Sal inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation.
source: The results in Figure 5B show that Sal inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription initiation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sal inhibits nucleotide addition in both primer-dependent transcription initiation and de novo transcription initiation.
source: Sal inhibits nucleotide addition in both primer-dependent transcription initiation (Figure 5B) and de novo transcription initiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In primer-dependent transcription initiation, Sal inhibits all nucleotide-addition steps, including the first nucleotide-addition step to form a 3-nt RNA product from a 2-nt RNA primer and an NTP.
source: In primer-dependent transcription initiation, Sal inhibits all nucleotide-addition steps, including the first nucleotide-addition step to form a 3-nt RNA product from a 2-nt RNA primer and an NTP (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In de novo transcription initiation, Sal inhibits all nucleotide-addition steps, including the first nucleotide-addition step to form a 2-nt RNA product from NTPs.
source: In de novo transcription initiation, Sal inhibits all nucleotide-addition steps, including the first nucleotide-addition step to form a 2-nt RNA product from NTPs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Rif, which does not inhibit the first nucleotide-addition step in transcription initiation.
source: The results indicate that the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Rif, which does not inhibit the first nucleotide-addition step in transcription initiation (Figure 5B; McClure and Cech, 1978).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citation to prior work on Rif (McClure and Cech, 1978).

claim: Sal inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription elongation.
source: The results in Figure 5C show that Sal also inhibits nucleotide addition in transcription elongation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In transcription elongation, Sal inhibits nucleotide addition both at non-pause sites and at type-I and type-II pause sites.
source: In transcription elongation, Sal inhibits nucleotide addition both at non-pause sites (Figure 5C) and at type-I and type-II pause sites (hairpin-stabilized pauses and backtracking-stabilized pauses; Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sal inhibits not only the forward reaction of nucleotide addition but also the reverse reaction, pyrophosphorolysis.
source: In transcription elongation, Sal inhibits nucleotide addition both at non-pause sites (Figure 5C) and at type-I and type-II pause sites (hairpin-stabilized pauses and backtracking-stabilized pauses; Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and inhibits not only the forward reaction of nucleotide addition but also the reverse reaction, pyrophosphorolysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanisms of transcription inhibition by Rif, Myx, and Lpm, which do not inhibit transcription elongation.
source: The results confirm that the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanisms of transcription inhibition by Rif, Myx, and Lpm, which do not inhibit transcription elongation (Figure 5C; McClure and Cech, 1978; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Tupin et al., 2010; Srivastava et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C and citations to prior work on Rif, Myx, and Lpm.

claim: Inhibition by Sal is noncompetitive with respect to NTP substrate.
source: The results in Figure 5D show that inhibition by Sal is noncompetitive with respect to NTP substrate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Ki for inhibition by Sal is 0.2 µM.
source: The Ki for inhibition is 0.2 µM, which is equal to the IC50 for inhibition of transcription (compare Figures 5C and 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Sal does not inhibit the NTP binding sub-reaction of the nucleotide-addition cycle.
source: The results indicate that Sal does not inhibit the NTP binding sub-reaction of the nucleotide-addition cycle, but instead inhibits one or more of the bond-formation, pyrophosphate-release, and translocation sub-reactions of the nucleotide-addition cycle.
evidence: Inference based on noncompetitive inhibition kinetics shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Sal inhibits one or more of the bond-formation, pyrophosphate-release, and translocation sub-reactions of the nucleotide-addition cycle.
source: The results indicate that Sal does not inhibit the NTP binding sub-reaction of the nucleotide-addition cycle, but instead inhibits one or more of the bond-formation, pyrophosphate-release, and translocation sub-reactions of the nucleotide-addition cycle.
evidence: Inference based on noncompetitive inhibition kinetics shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Transcription inhibition by Sal does not require the RNAP trigger loop.
source: The results in Figure 5E show that transcription inhibition by Sal does not require the RNAP active-center subregion referred to as the 'trigger loop'.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Sal inhibits wild-type RNAP and an RNAP-derivative having a deletion of the trigger loop to the same extent and with nearly the same concentration-dependence.
source: Thus, Sal inhibits wild-type RNAP and an RNAP-derivative having a deletion of the trigger loop to the same extent and with nearly the same concentration-dependence.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Stl, which absolutely requires the RNAP trigger loop.
source: These results indicate that the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal differs from the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Stl, which absolutely requires the RNAP trigger loop (Temiakov et al., 2005).
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5E and citation to prior work on Stl (Temiakov et al., 2005).

claim: Sal inhibits RNAP through a mechanism different from the mechanisms of the previously characterized RNAP inhibitors Rif, Stl, Myx, and Lpm.
source: Taken together, the results in Figure 5 establish that Sal inhibits RNAP through a mechanism different from the mechanisms of the previously characterized RNAP inhibitors Rif, Stl, Myx, and Lpm.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sal inhibits RNAP through a novel binding site and a novel mechanism.
source: Based on the data presented to this point, we suggest that Sal inhibits RNAP through a novel binding site and a novel mechanism.
evidence: Inference based on the combined genetic, biochemical, and structural data presented.

claim: Sal interacts with a binding site in the bridge-helix cap and allosterically interferes with the conformational dynamics of the BH-HN required for one or more of bond formation, pyrophosphate release, and translocation in the nucleotide-addition cycle.
source: Specifically, we suggest that Sal interacts with a binding site in the bridge-helix cap and allosterically interferes with the conformational dynamics of the BH-HN required for one or more of bond formation, pyrophosphate release, and translocation in the nucleotide-addition cycle of transcription initiation and transcription elongation.
evidence: Inference based on the combined genetic, biochemical, and structural data presented.

claim: The crystal structure of E. coli RNAP holoenzyme was determined at 3.9 Å resolution.
source: Figure 6A shows the resulting crystal structure of E. coli RNAP holoenzyme at 3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The crystal structure of E. coli RNAP holoenzyme in complex with Sal was determined at 3.9 Å resolution.
source: Figures 6B and C show the corresponding structure of E. coli RNAP holoenzyme in complex with Sal at 3.9 Å resolution.
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figures 6B and C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The structure of E. coli RNAP holoenzyme in complex with Sal shows unambiguous experimental electron density for Sal in the genetically-defined Sal target.
source: The structure shows unambiguous experimental electron density for Sal in the genetically-defined Sal target, confirming the hypothesis that the genetically-defined Sal target represents the binding site for Sal on RNAP (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figures 6B and C.

claim: Sal–Br was prepared by semi-synthesis from SalA, exploiting the unique chemical reactivity of the residue-9 epoxide moiety of SalA.
source: Sal–Br was prepared by semi-synthesis from SalA, exploiting the unique chemical reactivity of the residue-9 epoxide moiety of SalA (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by chemical synthesis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Sal–Br exhibits essentially full RNAP-inhibitory activity and essentially full antibacterial activity.
source: Sal–Br was found to exhibit essentially full RNAP-inhibitory activity and essentially full antibacterial activity (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The RNAP–Sal–Br complex exhibited a single peak of Br anomalous difference density immediately adjacent to the electron density for Sal–Br, in the position expected for a Br atom covalently bonded to a carbon atom of the Sal–Br residue-9 bromohydrin.
source: The RNAP–Sal–Br complex exhibited electron density for Sal–Br matching the electron density in the RNAP–Sal complex for Sal (blue mesh in Figures 6C and 7C) and exhibited a single peak of Br anomalous difference density immediately adjacent to the electron density for Sal–Br, in the position expected for a Br atom covalently bonded to a carbon atom of the Sal–Br residue-9 bromohydrin (pink mesh in Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Sal binds within the RNAP bridge-helix cap, making direct interactions with the BH-HN, the fork loop, and the link region.
source: The structural information shows that Sal binds within the RNAP bridge-helix cap, making direct interactions with the BH-HN, the fork loop, and the link region (Figures 6C, 7C, and 8).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figures 6C, 7C, and 8.

claim: Sal makes direct interactions with all five residues at which substitutions conferring high-level (≥128-fold) Sal-resistance are obtained (β′ residues Arg738, Ala779, and Gly782, and β residues Asp675 and Asn677).
source: Sal makes direct interactions with all five residues at which substitutions conferring high-level (≥128-fold) Sal-resistance are obtained (β′ residues Arg738, Ala779, and Gly782, and β residues Asp675 and Asn677; red in Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Substitution of β′ residue Arg738 would be expected to disrupt an H-bond between RNAP and Sal.
source: Substitution of β′ residue Arg738 would be expected to disrupt an H-bond between RNAP and Sal (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Substitution of β′ residue Ala779 or Gly782 by any residue having a larger sidechain would be expected to introduce severe steric clash between RNAP and Sal.
source: Substitution of β′ residue Ala779 or Gly782 by any residue having a larger sidechain would be expected to introduce severe steric clash between RNAP and Sal (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Substitution of β residues Asp675 and Asn677 would be expected to disrupt both H-bonds and van der Waals interactions between RNAP and Sal.
source: Substitution of β residues Asp675 and Asn677 would be expected to disrupt both H-bonds and van der Waals interactions between RNAP and Sal (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Six of the RNAP residues that make direct contact with Sal are conserved across Gram-positive bacterial RNAP, Gram-negative bacterial RNAP, and human RNAP I, II, and III (β′ residues 739, 745, 778, 779, 782, and 785).
source: Six of the RNAP residues that make direct contact with Sal are conserved across Gram-positive bacterial RNAP, Gram-negative bacterial RNAP, and human RNAP I, II, and III (β′ residues 739, 745, 778, 779, 782, and 785; Figures 3B and 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3B and structural data shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Nine RNAP residues that contact Sal are conserved in Gram-positive bacterial RNAP and Gram-negative bacterial RNAP, but are not conserved in human RNAP I, II, and III (β′ residues 738, 744, 746, 747, 748, 775, and 781, and β residues 675 and 677).
source: Nine RNAP residues that contact Sal are conserved in Gram-positive bacterial RNAP and Gram-negative bacterial RNAP, but are not conserved, and indeed are radically different, in human RNAP I, II, and III (β′ residues 738, 744, 746, 747, 748, 775, and 781, and β residues 675 and 677; Figures 3B and 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3B and structural data shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: The observed interactions account for, and explain, the observation that Sal inhibits Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial RNAP, but does not inhibit human RNAP I, II, and III.
source: The observed interactions account for, and explain, the observation that Sal inhibits Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial RNAP, but does not inhibit human RNAP I, II, and III (Figure 1C).
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis of Sal-RNAP contacts and sequence conservation patterns.

claim: Sal binds within a approximately 2000 Å3 pocket formed by the RNAP BH-HN, the RNAP fork loop, and the RNAP link region.
source: Sal binds within a ∼2000 Å3 pocket formed by the RNAP BH-HN, the RNAP fork loop, and the RNAP link region (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Backbone atoms of residues that form the Sal binding pocket have superimposible conformations in RNAP holoenzyme in the absence of Sal and in RNAP holoenzyme in complex with Sal.
source: Backbone atoms of residues that form the pocket have superimposible conformations in RNAP holoenzyme in the absence of Sal and in RNAP holoenzyme in complex with Sal, indicating that the pocket pre-exists in RNAP holoenzyme in the absence of Sal.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison of RNAP with and without Sal.

claim: The Sal binding pocket pre-exists in RNAP holoenzyme in the absence of Sal.
source: Backbone atoms of residues that form the pocket have superimposible conformations in RNAP holoenzyme in the absence of Sal and in RNAP holoenzyme in complex with Sal, indicating that the pocket pre-exists in RNAP holoenzyme in the absence of Sal.
evidence: Inference based on structural comparison showing no conformational change upon Sal binding.

claim: The Sal binding pocket opens at one end onto the RNAP secondary channel and the RNAP active-center 'i+1' nucleotide binding site.
source: The pocket opens at one end onto the RNAP secondary channel and the RNAP active-center 'i+1' nucleotide binding site (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Sal likely enters the binding pocket from the RNAP secondary channel and/or the active-center i+1 nucleotide site.
source: It seems likely that Sal enters the pocket from the RNAP secondary channel and/or the active-center i+1 nucleotide site.
evidence: Inference based on the location of the pocket opening shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Within the binding pocket, Sal residues 4, 5, 7, and 8 interact with the RNAP BH-HN.
source: Within the binding pocket, Sal residues 4, 5, 7, and 8 interact with the RNAP BH-HN, Sal residues 1–3 and 6–7 interact with the RNAP fork loop, and Sal residues 8 and 9 interact with the RNAP link region (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Sal residues 1–3 and 6–7 interact with the RNAP fork loop.
source: Within the binding pocket, Sal residues 4, 5, 7, and 8 interact with the RNAP BH-HN, Sal residues 1–3 and 6–7 interact with the RNAP fork loop, and Sal residues 8 and 9 interact with the RNAP link region (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Sal residues 8 and 9 interact with the RNAP link region.
source: Within the binding pocket, Sal residues 4, 5, 7, and 8 interact with the RNAP BH-HN, Sal residues 1–3 and 6–7 interact with the RNAP fork loop, and Sal residues 8 and 9 interact with the RNAP link region (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Sal residue 9 is at the end of the pocket that opens onto the RNAP secondary channel and the active-center i+1 nucleotide binding site.
source: Sal residue 9 is at the end of the pocket that opens onto the RNAP secondary channel and the active-center i+1 nucleotide binding site (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: The Sal residue-9 epoxide and methyl moieties extend into the opening of the binding pocket and make no or limited interactions with RNAP.
source: The Sal residue-9 epoxide and methyl moieties extend into this opening and make no or limited interactions with RNAP (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: The crystal structure of the RNAP-Sal complex shows that Sal interacts with the RNAP BH-HN in an open (unbent) state.
source: The crystal structure shows that Sal interacts with the RNAP BH-HN in an open (unbent) state (Figure 9A), the same state that has been observed in previous crystal structures of RNAP and RNAP complexes (Zhang et al., 1999, 2012; Campbell et al., 2001; Vassylyev et al., 2002, 2007a, 2007b; Temiakov et al., 2005; Tuske et al., 2005; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Murakami, 2013; Zuo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013; Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 9A and comparison with prior structures.

claim: The open (unbent) BH-HN conformation observed in the RNAP-Sal complex is the same state that has been observed in previous crystal structures of RNAP and RNAP complexes.
source: The crystal structure shows that Sal interacts with the RNAP BH-HN in an open (unbent) state (Figure 9A), the same state that has been observed in previous crystal structures of RNAP and RNAP complexes (Zhang et al., 1999, 2012; Campbell et al., 2001; Vassylyev et al., 2002, 2007a, 2007b; Temiakov et al., 2005; Tuske et al., 2005; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Murakami, 2013; Zuo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013; Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior structural work and comparison shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The open (unbent) BH-HN conformation is different from the closed (bent) BH-HN conformation that has been observed in molecular dynamics simulations of nucleotide-addition reactions in transcription elongation complexes.
source: This conformation is different from the closed (bent) BH-HN conformation that has been observed in molecular dynamics simulations of nucleotide-addition reactions in transcription elongation complexes (Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior molecular dynamics simulation work (Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).

claim: The closed (bent) BH-HN conformation has been postulated to serve as a critical intermediate in the bond-formation, pyrophosphate-release, and/or translocation reactions of the nucleotide-addition cycle.
source: This conformation is different from the closed (bent) BH-HN conformation that has been observed in molecular dynamics simulations of nucleotide-addition reactions in transcription elongation complexes (Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013), and that has been postulated to serve as a critical intermediate in the bond-formation, pyrophosphate-release, and/or translocation reactions of the nucleotide-addition cycle (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hein and Landick, 2010; Weinzierl, 2010; Kireeva et al., 2012; Nedialkov et al., 2013).

claim: Sal interacts with an open (unbent) BH-HN conformational state.
source: We conclude that Sal interacts with an open (unbent) BH-HN conformational state, and we propose that, through its interactions with that state, it stabilizes that state and prevents conformational dynamics required for nucleotide addition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from structural analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: Sal stabilizes the open (unbent) BH-HN conformational state and prevents conformational dynamics required for nucleotide addition.
source: We conclude that Sal interacts with an open (unbent) BH-HN conformational state, and we propose that, through its interactions with that state, it stabilizes that state and prevents conformational dynamics required for nucleotide addition.
evidence: Inference based on structural analysis and biochemical data showing inhibition of nucleotide addition.

claim: In the crystal structure of the RNAP-Sal complex, the RNAP trigger loop is disordered.
source: In the crystal structure of the RNAP-Sal complex, the RNAP trigger loop is disordered.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis of the RNAP-Sal complex.

claim: The structure of RNAP-Sal is compatible with the open (unfolded) trigger-loop conformations observed in crystal structures of RNAP and the transcription elongation complex without a bound NTP substrate.
source: Molecular modelling indicates that the structure of RNAP-Sal is compatible with the open (unfolded) trigger-loop conformations observed in crystal structures of RNAP and the transcription elongation complex without a bound NTP substrate (Zhang et al., 1999; Campbell et al., 2001; Vassylyev et al., 2002, 2007a; Temiakov et al., 2005; Tuske et al., 2005; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Murakami, 2013; Zuo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by molecular modeling and citations to prior structural work.

claim: The structure of RNAP-Sal would be incompatible with the closed (folded) trigger loop conformation observed in the crystal structure of the transcription elongation complex with a bound NTP substrate.
source: Molecular modelling indicates that the structure of RNAP-Sal is compatible with the open (unfolded) trigger-loop conformations observed in crystal structures of RNAP and the transcription elongation complex without a bound NTP substrate (Zhang et al., 1999; Campbell et al., 2001; Vassylyev et al., 2002, 2007a; Temiakov et al., 2005; Tuske et al., 2005; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2008; Belogurov et al., 2009; Murakami, 2013; Zuo et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013), but would be incompatible with the closed (folded) trigger loop conformation observed in the crystal structure of the transcription elongation complex with a bound NTP substrate (Vassylyev et al., 2007b; Figure 9C).
evidence: Supported by molecular modeling shown in Figure 9C and citation to prior structural work (Vassylyev et al., 2007b).

claim: Sal interacts with an open (unfolded) trigger-loop conformational state.
source: We infer that Sal interacts with an open (unfolded) trigger-loop conformational state, and likely would prevent the formation of the closed (folded) trigger-loop conformational state.
evidence: Inference based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Sal likely would prevent the formation of the closed (folded) trigger-loop conformational state.
source: We infer that Sal interacts with an open (unfolded) trigger-loop conformational state, and likely would prevent the formation of the closed (folded) trigger-loop conformational state.
evidence: Inference based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Effects of Sal on trigger-loop conformation may contribute to the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal.
source: It is possible that effects of Sal on trigger-loop conformation may contribute to the mechanism of transcription inhibition by Sal.
evidence: Speculation based on structural analysis.

claim: The trigger loop is not essential for transcription inhibition by Sal.
source: However, the results in Figure 5E show that the trigger loop is not essential for transcription inhibition by Sal, and therefore, although effects of Sal on trigger loop conformation may contribute to transcription inhibition by Sal, they cannot be essential for transcription inhibition by Sal.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Sal is the first RNAP inhibitor that has been proposed to function through effects on conformational dynamics of the BH-HN.
source: Sal is the first RNAP inhibitor that has been proposed to function through effects on conformational dynamics of the BH-HN.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with known RNAP inhibitors and their mechanisms.

claim: Sal will find use as a research tool for dissection of mechanistic and structural aspects of BH-HN conformational dynamics.
source: We suggest that Sal will find use as a research tool for dissection of mechanistic and structural aspects of BH-HN conformational dynamics.
evidence: Speculation about future applications based on the novel mechanism of Sal.

claim: The SalA epoxide moiety provides a chemical reactivity that can be exploited for semi-synthesis of novel Sal analogs.
source: The semi-synthesis of Sal–Br from SalA (Figure 7A) shows that the SalA epoxide moiety provides a chemical reactivity that can be exploited for semi-synthesis of novel Sal analogs.
evidence: Supported by chemical synthesis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Semi-synthetic modifications at the SalA epoxide moiety can be tolerated without loss of potency.
source: The retention of RNAP inhibitory activity and antibacterial activity by Sal–Br (Figure 7B) shows that semi-synthetic modifications at the SalA epoxide moiety can be tolerated without loss of potency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Introduction at the SalA epoxide moiety of a sidechain with negatively-charged functionality should enable new, energetically favorable, electrostatic interactions with positively-charged 'basic-rim' residues in the RNAP secondary channel.
source: Introduction at the SalA epoxide moiety of a sidechain with negatively-charged functionality should enable new, energetically favorable, electrostatic interactions with positively-charged 'basic-rim' residues in the RNAP secondary channel.
evidence: Speculation based on structural analysis showing the epoxide moiety is directed toward the secondary channel.

claim: Introduction at the Sal epoxide moiety of a nucleotide or nucleoside analog should enable new, energetically favorable, interactions with the RNAP active-center i+1 nucleotide binding site.
source: Introduction at the Sal epoxide moiety of a nucleotide or nucleoside analog, should enable new, energetically favorable, interactions with the RNAP active-center i+1 nucleotide binding site.
evidence: Speculation based on structural analysis showing the epoxide moiety is directed toward the i+1 nucleotide binding site.

claim: Covalently linking Sal to a nucleotide or nucleoside analog is expected to yield a bipartite inhibitor that interacts simultaneously with the Sal binding pocket and the active-center i+1 nucleotide binding site.
source: Covalently linking Sal to a nucleotide or nucleoside analog is expected to yield a bipartite inhibitor that interacts simultaneously with the Sal binding pocket and the active-center i+1 nucleotide binding site, and therefore, that potentially exhibits a very high affinity of binding and a very high potency of inhibition.
evidence: Speculation based on structural analysis.
